newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks expected to open lower.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are seen weak at the opening but analysts said they could move higher if Wednesday's bounce in the high techs is sustained.
Other factors include the bond market, which was flat ahead of the opening bell, and weekly jobless claims due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.

"I think the turnaround we saw yesterday offers hope and, unless something disturbing were to happen, the market should continue improving, especially if the techs hang in there," said Hildergard Zagorski, analyst at Prudential Securities.

"Yesterday, the whole market was lifted by the fact that the five-year Treasury auction was successful and, after the auction, the techs rallied," she said. "They were also going through a bounce because they were slammed the day before."
Thom Brown, managing director of Rutherford Brown and Catherwood, said he expected the market to stabilize today.

"We saw the rolling correction mostly in blue chips, and today the market will probably stabilize and pick up," Brown said. "It's encouraging that the techs were higher than the overall market yesterday and that other major averages did not get clipped as badly as the Dow Industrials."
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 79 points at 21,003.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 10 at 4018.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, General Motors Corp added 1/4 to 54-3/4. Anheuser-Busch Inc rose 1/4 to 39-3/8.
The dollar was off its highs in Japan and firm in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond down 5/32 to yield 6.84 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that many analysts and investors think that Signet Banking Corp should look for a company to take it over at a premium price in order to help it get back into shape.

The New York Times Marketplace said a ruling by the Delaware Supreme Court will probably put a damper on two-step mergers in which an acquirer gains control of a company before forcing a merger. The court ruled that a lower court had misinterpreted legal precedents in finding that the MacAndrews & Forbes Group, the buyout firm controlled by Ronald O. Perelman, paid an adequate price for Technicolor Inc in 1983.
